meta.regime: For two weeks this book traded an energy shock. Today a second, larger force arrived on top of it, and it came from the US Treasury rather than from any central bank. Washington announced it would DOUBLE the size of its liquidity-support buyback operations for longer-dated bonds, and the long end of the US curve broke: 30-year yields fell hard from around their highest level in nineteen years and the 10-year dropped toward the 4.6% area. That single administrative decision did what four soft data prints could not - it removed the real-rate anchor that had been holding the havens down. Gold rose 4.26% to 4,519.79, silver 5.84% to 67.016, platinum 5.73% to 1,833 and palladium 3.90%, all in one session. The dollar index is 98.826 and back at NEW LOWS, down 1.14% on the week, having briefly stabilised at 99.65 on Tuesday. And critically for this book, USD/CHF broke BELOW the 0.80 handle to 0.79946, with the franc up 1.78% on the week against the dollar and also firmer on the EUR/CHF cross at roughly 0.9336 against 0.9400 on Tuesday - so the haven bid whose absence forced Tuesday's CHF downgrade has now arrived. Two corrections follow: XAU and XAG return to HIGH conviction, and CHF is upgraded from -1 to 0. The energy leg has not gone away - Brent is heading toward 93 dollars with WTI at 85.78, the US says there are no ongoing negotiations with Tehran, the naval blockade stands and eight vessels have been attacked in Hormuz this month - so the oil-linked longs stay intact. What broke today was Australia: July employment FELL 15,800 against a consensus of plus 20 to 25 thousand, unemployment rose to 4.5% - the highest of the post-COVID era - participation dropped 0.2 points to 66.9% and the underutilisation rate rose to 10.8%. AUD goes to 0 and the Aussie crosses come down with it. The FOMC minutes were the day's ignored document: many participants judged that policy tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline, three presidents dissented for a hike, and the market simply looked through it in favour of the buyback.

dailyRead: Start with the mechanism, because everything today runs through it. The US Treasury said it would DOUBLE the size of its liquidity-support buyback operations for longer-dated bonds. Thirty-year yields, which had been sitting around a nineteen-year high, fell sharply, and the 10-year dropped toward the 4.6% area. Long US real rates are the single most important input into the price of gold and the value of the dollar, and both repriced instantly. Gold rose 4.26% to 4,519.79 dollars, its highest since early June. Silver rose 5.84% to 67.016. Platinum rose 5.73% to 1,833 and palladium 3.90% to 1,344. The dollar index fell back to 98.826 and is down 1.14% on the week, having stopped making lows only briefly on Tuesday at 99.65. This is the correction to Tuesday's file: I wrote then that the metals had refused the haven role and that the dollar short was stalling into Jackson Hole. Both of those statements were true for one session and are now false. XAU goes back UP to HIGH, XAG UP to HIGH, and DXY UP to HIGH. The second correction is the Swiss franc, and it matters more for the crosses. On Tuesday USD/CHF was 0.81165 and Trading Economics had the franc at a nearly one-year low with the SNB intervening explicitly to limit safe-haven inflows. Today USD/CHF is 0.79946 - through the 0.80 handle and down 1.78% on the week - and the franc is stronger on the euro cross too, with EUR/CHF near 0.9336 against 0.9400 on Tuesday. A franc that appreciates against BOTH the dollar and the euro in a week when long yields collapse and gold gains 4% is catching a genuine haven bid, not being pushed around by a weak dollar. CHF is upgraded from -1 to 0 MIXED. That does not make the Swiss data hawkish - July CPI at 0.4% is a four-month low, core is 0.3%, producer and import prices are still deflating at -2.1% y/y, the policy rate is 0.00% with the next assessment on September 24 and the consensus sees no hike before 2028 - but the SNB explicitly warned in June that Middle East tensions could strengthen the franc, and that is now happening. The practical effect: USD/CHF becomes a MEDIUM SHORT rather than a RANGE, EUR/CHF and CAD/CHF come DOWN from HIGH, and AUD/CHF and NZD/CHF go to RANGE because both legs now sit at zero. The dollar itself moves back DOWN to -2 WEAKENING. The four-print deterioration is unchanged - payrolls MINUS 23,000 with 146,000 of downward revisions, CPI 3.4% with core 2.5% at a five-month low, PPI 4.7%, retail sales -0.6% with the control group -0.4% - and now the long end of the curve has been administratively pushed lower on top of it. Wednesday's FOMC minutes were hawkish and were ignored: many participants assessed that policy tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline, some judged financial conditions might not be tight enough to return inflation to 2%, and Hammack, Kashkari and Logan each dissented for a quarter-point hike out of a 9-3 vote. The minutes also recorded Chair Warsh proposing to cut the FOMC calendar from eight meetings to six. None of it moved the tape. Jackson Hole on August 27 is still the reversal risk and crude at 85.78 still hands Warsh an inflation argument, but for now the dollar short is working again and should be pressed rather than trimmed. Australia is the day's casualty and the downgrade is not marginal. July employment FELL 15,800 against a consensus of plus 20 to 25 thousand, after June had printed +76,343. Full-time work rose 16,300 but part-time collapsed 32,200. The unemployment rate rose to 4.5% from 4.4%, the highest of the post-COVID era. The participation rate fell 0.2 points to 66.9% and the employment-to-population ratio fell 0.2 to 63.9%, so the unemployment rate would have been worse had people not left the labour force. Underutilisation rose to 10.8% and underemployment to 6.4%. Set that against consumer inflation expectations that had already collapsed to 4.7% from 5.5% in July, wage growth at 3.2%, quarterly GDP at 0.3% and job vacancies down to 330,000, and the hawkish RBA frame is now carried entirely by the 4.35% cash rate and Bullock's statement that the Board discussed only hike-or-hold. AUD drops from +1 to 0 MIXED. AUD/NZD and AUD/CHF go to RANGE, EUR/AUD and GBP/AUD are upgraded, and AUD/USD survives as a LONG only because the dollar leg is doing the work. The one genuine positive: consumer confidence jumped to 88.9 in August from 83.9, a 6% monthly gain. New Zealand goes the other way and completes Tuesday's correction. NZD/USD is 0.59520, UP 0.27% today and UP 1.74% on the week - the best G10 performer of the week after being the worst performer on Tuesday. The reason is policy: Governor Anna Breman said the Official Cash Rate is likely to rise SOONER AND MORE SHARPLY than the Bank had previously indicated, and Trading Economics has markets expecting another 25bp on September 2 after the July move to 2.50%. The data is also turning: business confidence JUMPED to 56.1 in July from 36.6, the ANZ Roy Morgan consumer confidence index rose to 99.3 from 91.3, and the Global Dairy Trade index rose 2.3% in August after just 0.1%. The hard numbers are still poor - unemployment 5.6% and the highest since 2015, wage growth 2.1%, two-year inflation expectations 2.34% - but a central bank promising to move faster with confidence surveys turning is worth an upgrade. NZD goes from -1 to 0. NZD/USD becomes a LONG, NZD/JPY becomes a LONG, and the NZD/CAD short comes down to LOW-MED. The United Kingdom delivered exactly the print this book warned about and the market read it correctly. July CPI rose to 2.9% from 2.6%, the first increase in the annual rate since March, driven by gas prices surging 14.7% month-on-month - the biggest jump since October 2022 - and electricity up 3.6% on the Ofgem cap. That is a mechanical, administered increase. Underneath it, core CPI held at 2.6% and services inflation COOLED to 3.4% from 3.6%. Monday's labour report was soft in the same direction: wage growth eased to 4.1% from 4.4%, employment change fell to +83,000 from +147,000. Sterling barely moved on either, sitting at 1.36069 and up 0.90% on the week entirely on the dollar leg. GBP holds +1 on the strength of the 3.75% Bank Rate, the three MPC dissenters and the G10-highest gilt, but the hawkish case is thinning and October brings another energy cap adjustment. Canada comes DOWN from +2 to +1, and this is a genuine reassessment rather than a mood swing. The July CPI story is intact and strong - headline 3.0%, energy inflation 16.6% from 14.3%, CPI-median 2.0%, trim 1.9%, common 2.7%, core 2.3%, services 2.5%, all higher - and the labour market is the G10s best with +75,100 jobs and unemployment at a two-year low of 6.4%. But the activity data has quietly deteriorated: the composite PMI is 49.7 and the services PMI 49.1, both in CONTRACTION, GDP annual growth is -0.1%, the terms of trade fell to 101 from 107, and business confidence slipped to 55.1 from 56.2. A central bank at 2.25% with sub-50 PMIs will not tighten into that, whatever the CPI says. CAD stays a buy against the dollar and the yen; it stops being a top-tier currency. USD/CAD comes down from HIGH to MEDIUM, CAD/CHF from HIGH to LOW-MED, EUR/CAD flips from RANGE to a LOW-MED LONG. The euro keeps +2 and remains the best-supported score on the board, now for a second reason. July HICP is 2.9% with core UP to 2.5%, services 3.3%, energy HICP accelerating to 10.0% from 8.5%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, wage growth 3.4%, unemployment 6.3%, the composite PMI back to 52.0 and the euro-area ZEW jumping to 31.4 in August from 23.4. Trading Economics calls the September 10 hike almost fully priced and says only a material easing in energy prices would change that - with Brent heading toward 93, that condition is nowhere near met. The deposit facility is re-verified at 2.25% against the 2.40% refi headline and 2.65% marginal lending. The ECB Monetary Policy Meeting Accounts land at 09:30Z today and are the one thing that could soften the pricing. Japan stays -1 MIXED but the balance improved. USD/JPY is 158.506, UP 0.21% today but DOWN 0.62% on the week and comfortably away from the 160 line where the MoF has already acted. The 10-year JGB remains near multi-decade highs and roughly 62% is priced for a hike to 1.25% on September 18. Against that, the import price index is at a record 200 with import prices up 29.1% y/y, terms of trade have fallen to 81.62, the trade balance is -407 billion yen and the current account swung to -923 billion. July national CPI at 23:30Z tonight, with core expected at 1.8% from 1.6% and Tokyo already at 1.9%, is the decider for September; the trade balance follows at 23:50Z. Trade the yen through EUR/JPY and CAD/JPY where the other leg is strong, and keep USD/JPY a MEDIUM short now that the dollar leg has re-engaged. Finally the commodity complex. USOIL stays a HIGH-conviction LONG: WTI 85.776 up 0.98%, Brent 91.592 heading toward 93 and up more than 4% on the week, with President Trump saying there are no ongoing negotiations with Tehran, the US naval blockade still in effect, eight attacks on Hormuz-transiting vessels this month including UAE and Saudi-linked ships, and the EIA seeing no return to pre-conflict Middle East output until early 2027. Copper is the outlier that did NOT join the metals melt-up - up just 0.29% to 6.5013 and DOWN 1.45% on the week - which is exactly what you would expect if this is a real-rate and haven trade rather than a growth trade, so XCU stays RANGE. GER40 at 26,091 and down 0.14% is caught between a collapsing global discount rate, which helps, and Brent at 92 plus a September ECB hike, which hurt; it moves from SHORT to RANGE.

USD.when: Sept 16 FOMC (hold still the base case - but the curve just moved without the Fed)
USD.note: Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 in a 9-3 vote, with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan each dissenting for a quarter-point hike. Re-verified on TE this morning: policy rate 3.75% upper bound, CPI 3.4% from 3.5%, core 2.5% from 2.6% and a five-month low, Q2 GDP 1.5% annualised with annual growth 2.1%, unemployment 4.1% from 4.2%, non-farm payrolls MINUS 23,000 from +20,000, average hourly earnings +0.1% m/m, retail sales -0.6% m/m, PPI 4.7% from 5.5%, core PCE 3.3% y/y, headline PCE 3.7%, consumer confidence 51.0 in August from 55.2, initial claims 209,000. Wednesday's FOMC minutes were the most hawkish document of the month and the market discarded them: many participants assessed that policy tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline, and some judged that financial conditions might not be tight enough to return inflation to 2%. The minutes also record Chair Warsh proposing to reduce the FOMC calendar from eight meetings to six, on the argument that a roughly two-monthly cadence would let more information accumulate between decisions. What overwhelmed all of it was fiscal plumbing rather than monetary policy: the Treasury said it would DOUBLE the size of liquidity-support buyback operations for longer-dated bonds, 30-year yields fell sharply from around a nineteen-year high, the 10-year dropped toward 4.6%, and the dollar index went straight back to new lows at 98.826, down 1.14% on the week. Lower long real rates with unchanged policy is the cleanest possible dollar-negative and gold-positive combination, which is exactly what the tape delivered. USD moves back DOWN to -2 and the dollar short should be pressed rather than trimmed. Jackson Hole on Aug 27 remains the single reversal risk, and with crude at 85.78 Warsh still has an energy argument available. July core PCE lands Aug 26.

EUR.when: Sept 10 (TE: almost fully priced - and energy is still not easing)
EUR.note: Deposit facility 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike, the first in three years, with main refinancing at 2.40% and marginal lending at 2.65%, all confirmed unchanged on Jul 23 and re-verified on TE this morning. Use the 2.25% depo, not the 2.40% headline. The domestic case is unchanged and is now the most self-supporting on the board: July HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5% from 2.4% and services inflation 3.3% from 3.2%, energy HICP accelerating to 10.0% from 8.5%, Q2 GDP confirmed at +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y with annualised growth 1.8%, composite PMI back to 52.0 from 50.0, services PMI 51.7 from 49.4, wage growth 3.4% from 3.1%, unemployment 6.3% and stable, and the euro-area ZEW jumping to 31.4 in August from 23.4. TE calls the September move almost fully priced and says that unless energy prices ease materially that view is unlikely to change - with Brent at 91.59 and heading toward 93, they are not easing. Lagarde's justification has always been that the longer energy prices stay elevated the more likely they drive broader inflation through indirect and second-round effects, and Canada has already published the hard proof of that channel working. The ECB Monetary Policy Meeting Accounts land TODAY at 09:30Z and are the single thing that could soften the pricing: they will show how the wait-and-see language was actually agreed after the July hold, and a softer internal consensus than the market assumes is the main risk to the euro's +2. The standing cautions stand: consumer inflation expectations fell to 3.0% from 3.5%, producer prices decelerated to 4.6% y/y, retail sales were -0.3% m/m and food inflation is down to 0.8%. EUR/USD is 1.16778 and up 1.30% on the week.

GBP.when: Sept 17 (Jul 30 = 6-3 hold; both of this week's prints came in soft underneath)
GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus, verified on TE today, with TE's end-of-quarter model still at 4.00%. Both decisive prints have now landed and both cut the same way once you look past the headline. Monday's labour report: wage growth eased to 4.1% including bonuses from 4.4%, employment change fell to +83,000 from +147,000, unemployment held at 4.9%, and the claimant count actually FELL 11,000 after a 6,400 fall. Wednesday's July CPI rose to 2.9% from 2.6%, the first increase in the annual rate since March - but the driver was administered energy, with gas prices up 14.7% month-on-month, the biggest jump since October 2022, and electricity up 3.6% on the Ofgem cap adjustment. Core CPI held at 2.6%, above the 2.5% consensus but not rising, and services inflation COOLED to 3.4% from 3.6%. Producer prices decelerated to 3.1% from 3.5%. Sterling and gilt futures barely moved on either release; cable is 1.36069 and up 0.90% on the week almost entirely on the dollar leg. The underlying picture is a decent but decelerating economy: Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q with the annual rate up to 1.2% but the quarterly rate down from 0.6%, composite PMI 52.2 from 49.3, retail sales +1.0% m/m. The 10-year gilt near 5.1% is still the G10's highest and is doing more for sterling than the MPC is. GBP holds +1, but with services inflation falling and wages easing, the three dissenters are running out of evidence, and another Ofgem adjustment arrives in October. Express sterling against the yen and the dollar rather than against the euro.

JPY.when: Sept 18 (~62% priced - tonight's CPI decides it)
JPY.note: Held 1.00% on Jul 31 8-1, Takata dissenting for 1.25%, verified on TE. The Q2 GDP miss - 0.3% q/q against 0.5%, 1.1% annualised against 2.0%, with flat private consumption - has not dented the rate market: the 10-year JGB sits near multi-decade highs and roughly 62% remains priced for a hike to 1.25% on September 18. The currency picture improved this week: USD/JPY is 158.506, up 0.21% today but DOWN 0.62% on the week, which pulls it away from the 160 level where the MoF has already demonstrated it will act. The structural problem is unchanged and is entirely about energy. The import price index printed a record 200 from 197 with import prices up 29.1% y/y, export prices are 163, terms of trade have deteriorated to 81.62 from 82.71, the trade balance is -JPY 407bn and the current account swung to -JPY 923bn from +3,968bn. Brent at 91.59 makes every one of those worse each month. The domestic case remains the best in three decades: June labour cash earnings +3.4% y/y, real earnings including bonuses +1.6% and positive for a sixth month, June CPI 1.7% with core 1.6% and core-core 1.7%, Tokyo July CPI 2.0% and Tokyo core 1.9%, PPI 7.2%, inflation expectations 2.7%, unemployment 2.5%, jobs-to-applications 1.18, June industrial output +1.9% m/m and +4.9% y/y, machinery orders +9.7% m/m and +16.9% y/y, and the Reuters Tankan rising to 18 in August from 13. The July Summary of Opinions was the most hawkish document of this cycle - one member said the pace of hikes could EXCEED market expectations, another that the cost of delay is not insignificant, another that inflation risks are skewed sharply to the upside as higher oil costs feed through. July national CPI lands TONIGHT at 23:30Z with core expected at 1.8% from 1.6%, and the trade balance follows at 23:50Z.

AUD.when: Sept 29 (the hawkish hold just lost its labour-market justification)
AUD.note: Held the cash rate at 4.35% on Aug 11 in a UNANIMOUS decision, verified on TE today, with Governor Bullock revealing the Board did NOT discuss a cut at all - only whether to raise or hold - and saying another hike was possible. That frame took real damage this morning. The July labour force survey, released at 01:30Z, showed employment FELL 15,800 against a consensus of plus 20 to 25 thousand and after June's +76,343. Full-time employment rose 16,300 but part-time collapsed 32,200. The unemployment rate rose to 4.5% from 4.4%, the highest of the post-COVID era. The participation rate fell 0.2 points to 66.9% and the employment-to-population ratio fell 0.2 points to 63.9%, so the rise in unemployment understates the deterioration - people left the labour force. Underemployment rose to 6.4% and underutilisation to 10.8%. That lands on top of a cluster that was already pointing down: consumer inflation expectations COLLAPSED to 4.7% in July from 5.5%, wage growth is 3.2%, quarterly GDP slowed to 0.3% from 0.9%, job vacancies fell to 330,000 from 338,000, the terms of trade dropped to 112 from 117, business confidence is -6 and the current account deficit is a record -AUD 27.1bn. What is left of the hawkish case is the rate itself and the price data: 4.35% is still the G10's highest, Q2 weighted median CPI ROSE to 3.7% and services inflation to 4.0%, trimmed mean 3.6%, headline 3.8%, commodity prices +15.4% y/y, composite PMI 53.2 and services 53.6, and consumer confidence jumped to 88.9 in August from 83.9. That is enough to keep the RBA on hold on September 29 but not enough to keep the Aussie in the top half of the board. AUD moves from +1 to 0 MIXED.

NZD.when: Sept 2 (Breman: sooner AND more sharply than indicated)
NZD.note: The OCR was raised 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years, verified on TE. Tuesday's file upgraded the kiwi from -2 to -1 on TE's observation that markets expect another quarter-point in September; today it goes to 0, and the reason is the Governor's own words. Anna Breman said in a speech that the Official Cash Rate is likely to rise SOONER AND MORE SHARPLY than the Bank had previously indicated - that is a deliberate escalation of the July guidance, not a restatement of it, and TE has markets widely expecting another 25bp on September 2. The survey data has turned with it: business confidence JUMPED to 56.1 in July from 36.6, the ANZ Roy Morgan consumer confidence index rose to 99.3 from 91.3, the Global Dairy Trade index rose 2.3% in August after only 0.1% in the prior auction, and food inflation eased to 1.9% from 2.5%. The price backdrop justifies the Bank: Q2 CPI accelerated to 4.1% from 3.1%, well above the 1-3% target band, with core at 3.2%. The hard activity data is still the G10's worst and that is why this is an upgrade to zero and not further: unemployment 5.6% and the highest since Q3 2015 with 171,000 unemployed, wage growth just 2.1%, youth unemployment 17.2%, the manufacturing PMI down to 54.3 from 60.1, the services PMI 50.6, two-year inflation expectations at 2.34%, ANZ commodity prices +0.5% and job vacancies down to 154. But the tape has already voted: NZD/USD is 0.59520, UP 0.27% today and UP 1.74% on the week - the best G10 performer of the week, after being the worst on Tuesday. NZD/USD and NZD/JPY become LONGs, NZD/CHF goes RANGE, and the NZD/CAD short comes down to LOW-MED.

CAD.when: Sept 2 (hold - and the PMIs now argue against the hike camp)
CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting, re-verified on TE. The inflation case made on Tuesday is intact and was correctly called: July CPI rebounded to 3.0% from 2.8%, at the ceiling of the Bank's 1-3% control range, with energy inflation accelerating to 16.6% from 14.3% on gasoline, and every core measure higher - CPI-median 2.0% from 1.9%, CPI-trim 1.9%, CPI-common 2.7% from 2.6%, core ex food and energy 2.3% from 2.1%, services inflation 2.5% from 2.2%, goods 3.7% from 3.5%. The labour market is the G10's best: July employment +75,100, the largest gain in two years, full-time +38,600, unemployment down to a two-year low of 6.4%, participation 65.1%, employment rate 60.9%. What forces the downgrade from +2 to +1 is the activity side, which this book under-weighted on Tuesday. The composite PMI is 49.7 and the services PMI is 49.1 - both in CONTRACTION - annual GDP growth is -0.1% with the quarterly rate at 0.0%, the terms of trade fell to 101 from 107 despite the oil move, business confidence slipped to 55.1 from 56.2, and house prices are -2.4% y/y. A central bank whose policy rate is already near the LOWER end of its estimated neutral range will not tighten into contracting services activity no matter what the CPI prints, and wage growth at 3.4% gives it no reason to. The asymmetry still runs away from cuts, which is why CAD stays positive - but it is no longer a top-tier currency. USD/CAD is 1.37952 and down 0.97% on the week, which is the smallest G10 gain against a dollar that fell 1.14%. June retail sales land Friday at 12:30Z; the next CPI is Sept 14, after the Sept 2 decision.

CHF.when: Sept 24 SNB (zero through 2027 - but the haven bid the SNB warned about has arrived)
CHF.note: CORRECTION to Tuesday's file. Policy rate 0.00%, verified on TE, with the next assessment on September 24 and TE's model at 0.00% through 2027. On Tuesday USD/CHF was 0.81165, TE described the franc as at a nearly one-year low, and the stated reason was SNB intervention limiting safe-haven inflows - so this book downgraded CHF to -1 and upgraded every franc-short cross. That call was right for one session and is wrong now. USD/CHF has broken BELOW the 0.80 handle to 0.79946, down 1.78% on the week, and the franc is firmer on the euro cross too, with EUR/CHF near 0.9336 against 0.9400 on Tuesday. Appreciation against BOTH the dollar and the euro, in the same week that 30-year US yields collapsed and gold gained 4.26%, is a haven bid rather than a dollar story. The SNB itself flagged exactly this risk in its June assessment: it named Middle East tensions as a global risk that could potentially strengthen the Swiss franc, alongside uncertain US trade policy, and signalled a greater readiness to intervene in FX if needed. It is now happening. CHF is upgraded from -1 to 0 MIXED. The domestic data has NOT changed and remains that of a funding currency: July CPI 0.4% from 0.5% and a four-month low, core 0.3%, producer and import prices deflating at -2.1% y/y, unemployment 3.0%, manufacturing PMI at a five-month low, consumer morale below expectations, the 10-year near 0.39%. The Q2 GDP shock at +1.5% q/q, the strongest since 2021, is pharma-distorted by exporters front-running US tariffs. The consensus sees no SNB hike before 2028 and the SNB's own inflation forecast is 0.6% for 2026 and 2027. So this is a positioning upgrade, not a policy one: USD/CHF becomes a MEDIUM SHORT, EUR/CHF and CAD/CHF come DOWN, GBP/CHF stays LOW-MED, and AUD/CHF and NZD/CHF go to RANGE because both legs now sit at zero.

catalysts.note: Euro-area composite was 52.0 from 50.0 and UK composite 52.2 from 49.3. Watch the input-price gauges specifically - after Canada showed energy reaching core, this is Europe's first read on the same channel ahead of the Sept 10 ECB.

The consumer read behind Canada's downgrade to +1, and the direct test of whether the sub-50 composite PMI at 49.7 is showing up in actual demand. A miss confirms the BoC has no path to tightening on Sept 2.

Core PCE is 3.3% y/y with headline at 3.7%. The last inflation input the Fed gets before Jackson Hole and the final one that matters for September pricing - the FOMC minutes made clear many participants want a hike if inflation does not fall.

The single biggest event for the dollar and the only thing that reverses today's setup. The July minutes show many participants judging that tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline, and with crude at 85.78 and Brent near 93 Warsh has a live energy argument to point at.
Another 25bp to 2.75% is widely expected after Governor Breman said the OCR will rise sooner and more sharply than previously indicated. Delivery inverts NZD/CAD and resolves AUD/NZD.

Hold at 2.25% is the base case. July CPI at 3.0% with all four core measures higher argues one way, a composite PMI at 49.7 and services at 49.1 argue the other - the statement language decides whether CAD keeps its +1.

Eight vessels transiting Hormuz have been attacked this month, including UAE and Saudi-linked ships. Brent is up more than 4% this week and the EIA sees no return to pre-conflict output until early 2027.

catalysts.event: SNB intervention watch as the franc breaks 0.80
catalysts.note: USD/CHF has broken BELOW 0.80 to 0.79946 with the franc also firmer against the euro. The SNB named Middle East tension in June as a risk that could strengthen the franc and signalled greater readiness to intervene - the first half has happened, so the second is now live.
USD/JPY at 158.506 is down 0.62% on the week and has moved away from the demonstrated MoF line, so this risk is dormant rather than dead - a soft CPI tonight would bring it straight back.

geopolitics: The energy shock is now the SECOND force in this book rather than the first, and that is today's most important structural change. It has not weakened - it has simply been joined by something larger. Crude is at 85.776 for WTI, up 0.98%, with Brent at 91.592 and heading toward 93, up more than 4% on the week and at the highest levels of the conflict. The positions have hardened rather than converged: President Trump has said there are NO ongoing negotiations with Tehran while confirming that the US naval blockade remains in effect, and Iran has repeated that the conditions for reopening the strait do not exist while the blockade continues. Eight vessels transiting Hormuz have been attacked so far this month, including ships linked to the UAE and Saudi Arabia. The interim peace memorandum signed in June expired on Monday and Trump has said he is not interested in extending it. Washington is not a party to the Iran-Oman corridor talks and will not support any arrangement that fails to guarantee unrestricted passage. The EIA does not expect Middle East production near pre-conflict levels until early 2027. What caps the price rather than resolving it is physical leakage - Gulf producers moving barrels covertly with transponders off and supplying cargoes from outside the chokepoint. The FX transmission now has four legs and one of them reversed today. First, the euro: euro-area energy HICP is accelerating at 10.0% from 8.5%, TE calls the Sept 10 ECB hike almost fully priced and says only materially easier energy would change that, and energy is not easing - this is the cleanest and most durable leg in the book. Second, Japan: the import price index printed a record 200 with import prices up 29.1% y/y, terms of trade fell to 81.62 and the current account swung to -JPY 923bn, so rising crude transmits into Japanese inflation and Japanese weakness at the same time - which is why tonight's CPI at 23:30Z matters so much. Third, Canada: the energy channel worked exactly as this book said it would, with July energy inflation at 16.6% and all four Bank of Canada core measures rising - but the activity data caught up, with the composite PMI at 49.7 and services at 49.1 both in contraction, so CAD comes down from +2 to +1. Fourth, and this is the reversal, the Swiss franc IS the escalation hedge after all. On Tuesday this book downgraded CHF because TE had it at a nearly one-year low with the SNB intervening to limit safe-haven inflows. Today USD/CHF has broken BELOW 0.80 to 0.79946, down 1.78% on the week, and the franc is firmer against the euro too. The SNB's own June assessment named Middle East tensions as a risk that could potentially strengthen the franc and signalled greater readiness to intervene - that is now playing out, and CHF is upgraded from -1 to 0. The wider haven complex confirms it: gold rose 4.26% to 4,519.79, silver 5.84% to 67.016, platinum 5.73% and palladium 3.90%, all on the same session that the US Treasury doubled its long-dated bond buybacks and drove 30-year yields down from a nineteen-year high. The one asset that refused to join was copper, up just 0.29% and down 1.45% on the week - which tells you this was a real-rate and haven repricing rather than a global growth impulse, and is why XCU stays RANGE while XAU and XAG go back to HIGH.
